questionsToConsider: Should the form be anonymous so people feel free to say a meeting was not worth it?
Which meetings are worth surveying: recurring ones, all-hands, or client meetings?
Do the grid rows match what you want from this meeting, such as brainstorming rather than decisions?
Who follows up when someone says the next steps are unclear?
guide.howToUseResponses: Act on unclear next steps the same day by sending a short written summary of who does what. For recurring meetings, watch the worth-your-time score across weeks and read what people say would work better: repeated votes for a written update suggest the meeting could become one. Look at the grid by role, since presenters and listeners often experience the same meeting very differently.
customizeSteps: Change the grid rows to match the meeting's purpose, and remove the role question if everyone plays the same part.
Prefill the meeting name from the link with a URL parameter so attendees don't have to type it each time.
Send the link at the end of the meeting or in the calendar follow-up, and review responses in the dashboard before the next one.

faqs.q: What questions should I ask after a meeting?
faqs.a: Whether it had a clear purpose, the right people and enough time to speak, whether it was worth attending, and whether everyone knows their next steps.
For internal meetings, usually yes. People are more honest about wasted time when their name is not attached. Keep the meeting name so you can still compare sessions.

faqs.q: When should I send a meeting feedback survey?
faqs.a: Within an hour of the meeting ending, while details are fresh. For a weekly meeting, asking every few weeks avoids survey fatigue.

faqs.q: How do I measure meeting effectiveness?
faqs.a: Track how many people say it was worth their time and how many leave with clear next steps. Both are easy to compare from one meeting to the next.
